claims.source: Imipenem	8	0.25	≥4
claims.evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with MIC data.

claims.claim: FK688 is resistant to meropenem (MIC = 4 µg/mL).
claims.source: Meropenem	4	0.03	≥4
claims.evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with MIC data.

claims.claim: The genome of FK688 does not encode KPC-2 carbapenemase.
claims.source: Our genome sequence analysis did not reveal a gene encoding KPC-2, the carbapenemase found in many K. quasipneumoniae isolates (Mathers et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genome sequence analysis and annotation.

claims.claim: DeepBL generated eight high-confidence predictions for β-lactamases in FK688.
claims.source: To identify any cryptic carbapenemases that may have escaped annotation, we made use of the machine learning predictor DeepBL (Wang et al., 2021). DeepBL identifies genes encoding β-lactamases of all types, including carbapenemases, and generated eight high-confidence predictions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the application of DeepBL to the genome sequence.

claims.claim: The two highest DeepBL predictions represent known β-lactamases blaOKP-B-21 and blaDHA-1.
claims.source: The two highest predictions represent known β-lactamases blaOKP-B-21 and blaDHA-1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by DeepBL analysis results.

claims.claim: Figure 1C shows that eight candidate β-lactamases were tested for carbapenemase activity in E. coli.
claims.source: (C) Eight candidate carbapenemases were identified in the FK688 genome sequence and overexpressed in an E. coli model of resistance. Only two enzymes (DHA1 and OKP-B-21) conferred resistance to the cephem antibiotics tested, and none of the enzymes conferred resistance to the carbapenem antibiotics (Figure 1—source data 6 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with MIC data for different antibiotics.

claims.claim: The position and synteny of each major porin gene in FK688 are conserved across K. quasipneumoniae.
claims.source: K. pneumoniae has four genes encoding the major porins OmpK35, OmpK36, OmpK37, and OmpK38 (Rocker et al., 2020), and the position and synteny of each gene in FK688 are conserved across K. quasipneumoniae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The structure of OmpK36 (PDB 5O79) is known.
claims.source: The structure of OmpK36 (PDB 5O79) is known (Acosta-Gutiérrez et al., 2018), and the identified deletion of 16 amino acids at the 3' end of the ompK36 gene in FK688 encompasses large portions of the β14 and β15 strands of the β-barrel structure (Figure 2A and Figure 2B), explaining why the protein is not assembled into the outer membrane of FK688.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Acosta-Gutiérrez et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The ompK36 gene from K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae ATCC 700603 was used to repair the OmpK36 gene in FK688.
claims.source: To confirm that this mutation was contributing to carbapenem resistance, we used the ompK36 gene from K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae ATCC 700603 (Elliott et al., 2016) to carry out structure-informed repair of the OmpK36 gene in K. quasipneumoniae FK688 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the genetic engineering approach described and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the restoration of OmpK36 expression in the ompK36+ pNAR1 strain.
claims.source: The resultant strain (ompK36+ pNAR1) was subjected to immunoblotting with antisera, confirming the restoration of OmpK36 expression in the ompK36+ pNAR1 strain (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: pNAR1 carries genes encoding AmpR, a transcriptional regulator known to regulate expression of blaDHA-1.
claims.source: In addition to blaDHA-1, pNAR1 carries genes encoding AmpR (ID00077) a transcriptional regulator known to regulate expression of blaDHA-1 (Realegeno et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genome annotation and a citation to Realegeno et al., 2021.

claims.claim: pNAR1 carries genes responsible for resistance to tetracycline, rifamycin, trimethoprim, streptomycin, macrolides, sulfonamides, and quinolones/fluoroquinolones.
claims.source: Also, other drug resistance genes including those responsible for resistance to tetracycline (tetA[B]), rifamycin (arr-3), trimethoprim (dfrA27), streptomycin (aadA16), macrolides (qacΔE1), sulfonamides (sul1), and quinolones and fluoroquinolones (qnrB4; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genome annotation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Whole genome sequencing established that the pNAR1‾ and pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1 strains had not sustained any other mutations.
claims.source: Whole genome sequencing established that the pNAR1‾ and pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1 strains had not sustained any other mutations, which confirmed the genotypes of strains ΔompK36 and ompK36+ with and without the plasmid-encoded blaDHA-1gene.
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing of the evolved strains.

claims.claim: At the breakpoint value of 0.125 µg/mL imipenem, three genotypes are at a selective disadvantage: ompK36+pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1, ompK36+pNAR1, and ΔompK36 pNAR1‾.
claims.source: At the breakpoint value of 0.125 µg/mL, three genotypes are already at a selective disadvantage: ompK36+pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1, ompK36+pNAR1, and ΔompK36 pNAR1‾.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fitness assays in imipenem shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Above the breakpoint value at 0.25 µg/mL imipenem, all four genotypes are at a selective disadvantage relative to the parental FK688.
claims.source: Above the breakpoint value at 0.25 µg/mL, all four genotypes are at a selective disadvantage relative to the parental FK688.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fitness assays in imipenem shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The ancestral FK688 strains (ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1) have an opaque colony morphology.
claims.source: The ancestral FK688 strains (ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1) have an opaque colony morphology.
claims.evidence: This is supported by colony morphology observations.

claims.claim: Non-fimbriated Klebsiella strains are mucoid due to capsule secretion and look opaque, while translucent colonies are fimbriated and non-mucoid.
claims.source: This is consistent with a phenotype of capsular polysaccharide production: non-fimbriated Klebsiella strains are mucoid due to capsule secretion and look opaque, while translucent colonies are fimbriated and non-mucoid (Matatov et al., 1999; Schembri et al., 2005; Wilksch et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Klebsiella colony morphology.

claims.claim: The fimE gene was not disrupted in the A2 population that was capable of phase-switching.
claims.source: The fimE gene was not disrupted in the A2 population that was capable of phase-switching (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Protein analysis of A2(o) and A2(t) by SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry showed no changes that were consistent in both populations to explain the increased sensitivity to imipenem.
claims.source: Protein analysis of A2(o) and A2(t) by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel (SDS-PAGE; Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 5) and mass spectrometry showed no changes that were consistent in both populations to explain the increased sensitivity to imipenem.
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Strains with an intact pNAR1 plasmid, including the blaDHA-1 gene, are able to survive high concentrations of ceftazidime.
claims.source: Only strains with an intact pNAR1 plasmid, including the blaDHA-1 gene, are able to survive high concentrations of ceftazidime.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with fitness data across ceftazidime concentrations.

claims.claim: The most logical starting point for evolution to carbapenem resistance is the genotype that does not have the blaDHA-1 gene or the loss of function mutation in ompK36, because it has the highest fitness in growth conditions without antibiotic.
claims.source: We evaluated the evolutionary path to antibiotic resistance by considering the starting point of evolution as the genotype that does not have the blaDHA-1 gene or the loss of function mutation in ompK36, indicated at "A". This genotype is the most logical starting point because it has the highest fitness in growth conditions without antibiotic (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the fitness data shown in Figure 4B.

results.result: FK688 is a clinical isolate of K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae, and this study presents the first complete genome assembly of this subspecies using hybrid sequencing approaches. The genome consists of a circular chromosome (5,211,811 bp) and a novel megaplasmid pNAR1 (1,257,585 bp).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C25, C30, C66, and C90 are well-supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1B), complete genome sequencing using long- and short-read data, and genome assembly results. The novelty claim (C66) is supported by the presentation of the first complete physical map for this subspecies.

results.result: FK688 does not encode a carbapenemase. Machine learning analysis using DeepBL identified eight candidate β-lactamases, but functional testing in E. coli showed that none conferred carbapenem resistance, though OKP-B-21 and DHA-1 conferred resistance to cephalosporins.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C34-C37, and C95-C98 are supported by comprehensive genome annotation, DeepBL machine learning predictions, and systematic MIC testing of all eight candidates expressed in E. coli (Figure 1C). The negative result for carbapenemase activity is well-documented through multiple independent lines of evidence.

results.result: Carbapenem resistance in FK688 requires two genetic loci: the megaplasmid pNAR1 carrying blaDHA-1 and an inactivating 48 bp deletion in the chromosomal ompK36 gene. The deletion removes 16 amino acids encompassing β14 and β15 strands, preventing OmpK36 assembly in the outer membrane. Genetic restoration of OmpK36 restored carbapenem sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C27, C39-C43, C48, and C74 are strongly supported by genome sequencing data, structural analysis using the known OmpK36 structure (PDB 5O79), genetic reconstruction experiments, immunoblotting (Figure 2D), and MIC testing (Table 2). The epistatic requirement of both loci is demonstrated through systematic testing of all genotype combinations.

results.result: Two distinct genetic loci are necessary for FK688 to acquire clinically relevant carbapenem resistance: the presence of DHA-1 β-lactamase and the absence of functional OmpK36 porin.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C51 are supported by genetic reconstruction experiments showing that both blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 are required for resistance at clinically relevant carbapenem concentrations (Figure 4C, Table 2). The claim is well-validated through systematic MIC testing and fitness assays across antibiotic concentration gradients.

results.result: Both genetic loci conferring carbapenem resistance impose significant fitness costs in the absence of antibiotics. Experimental evolution without antibiotic selection led to rapid loss of resistance through deletion of blaDHA-1 from pNAR1 or loss of the entire plasmid, restoring carbapenem sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C28, C44-C47, C49, C67, C75, and C76 are well-supported by mutation accumulation experiments (Figure 3), competitive fitness assays (Figure 4B), experimental evolution over 200 generations (Figure 5), and whole genome sequencing of evolved strains. The fitness costs and evolutionary reversibility are quantified and reproducible across multiple independent lineages.

results.result: Selection with ceftazidime can select for blaDHA-1 even at concentrations ~100× below the clinical breakpoint, potentiating the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single subsequent mutation in ompK36. The most likely evolutionary path is A→B→D, where prior ceftazidime exposure selects for pNAR1 (carrying blaDHA-1), enabling rapid evolution of carbapenem resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C29, C61-C65, C68, and C88 are supported by fitness assays across ceftazidime concentration gradients (Figure 6A), evolutionary potential experiments showing that only strains carrying blaDHA-1 can evolve imipenem resistance (Figure 6B), and the demonstration that ΔompK36 reduces fitness in ceftazidime. The sequential selection model is well-reasoned from the experimental data.

results.result: A patient's treatment history shapes the evolution of antibiotic resistance. The evolutionary history of a pathogenic strain predisposes it to evolve AMR via specific genetic routes, which should be considered when explaining the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C87, and C89 are supported by the experimental demonstration that prior selection for blaDHA-1 (e.g., through ceftazidime treatment) facilitates subsequent carbapenem resistance evolution. The inference is well-grounded in the fitness data and evolutionary experiments showing sequential selection for resistance alleles.

results.result: During experimental evolution without antibiotics, both ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1 populations independently evolved deletions in pNAR1 that removed blaDHA-1, recovering fitness costs and evolving increased carbapenem sensitivity (64-fold for ΔompK36 strains).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54, C59, and C60 are supported by fitness assays of evolved populations (Figure 5C), whole genome sequencing showing independent deletions of blaDHA-1, and MIC measurements (Table 3). The convergent evolution across independent lineages and the genetic reconstruction experiments (Table 2) strongly support the causal role of blaDHA-1 loss.

results.result: The fitness defects of blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 are gradually reversed in the presence of increasing imipenem concentrations. At the clinical breakpoint (0.125 µg/mL), three genotypes are at a selective disadvantage, and above 0.25 µg/mL, all four genotypes are disadvantaged relative to parental FK688.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C106, and C107 are supported by systematic fitness assays across imipenem concentration gradients (Figure 4C). The data clearly show the concentration-dependent reversal of fitness costs and identify specific breakpoints where different genotypes become selectively disadvantaged.

results.result: FK688 carries multiple antibiotic resistance determinants: chromosomal blaOKP-B-21 (conferring resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins), oqxA/oqxB (quinolone resistance), fosA5 (fosfomycin resistance), and plasmid-encoded blaDHA-1, AmpR, and genes for resistance to tetracycline, rifamycin, trimethoprim, streptomycin, macrolides, sulfonamides, and quinolones/fluoroquinolones.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33, C71, C72, C91, C103, and C104 are supported by genome annotation, functional testing (Figure 1C for β-lactamases), and citations to relevant literature. The resistance profile is consistent with the known phenotype and is well-documented through multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: After 200 generations of evolution, populations displayed a mixture of opaque and translucent colony morphotypes. This variation depends on type 1 fimbriae expression, with opaque colonies being non-fimbriated and mucoid (higher capsular polysaccharide), while translucent colonies are fimbriated and non-mucoid. In B3(o), a transposase insertion disrupted fimE.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C108-C110 are supported by colony morphology observations (Figure 5B, 5D), genome sequencing showing the fimE disruption (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), glucuronic acid measurements (Figure 5E), and citations to previous studies on Klebsiella colony morphology. The phenotypic and genetic data are consistent and well-documented.

results.result: FK688 is resistant to carbapenems with MICs of 64 µg/mL for ertapenem, 8 µg/mL for imipenem, and 4 µg/mL for meropenem, all exceeding clinical breakpoints for resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are directly supported by MIC data presented in Table 1, performed according to CLSI guidelines with appropriate quality controls (E. coli ATCC 25922). The measurements are clear and reproducible.

results.result: K. pneumoniae has four major porin genes (ompK35, ompK36, ompK37, ompK38) with conserved position and synteny in FK688. The structure of OmpK36 (PDB 5O79) is known, and the ompK36 gene from K. quasipneumoniae ATCC 700603 was used to repair the deletion in FK688, with restoration confirmed by immunoblotting.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C99-C102 are supported by comparative genomics (Figure 2—figure supplements), citation to the known OmpK36 structure, description of the genetic engineering approach (Figure 2C), and immunoblotting data (Figure 2D). The methods and results are well-documented.

results.result: In FK688, efflux pumps did not contribute to carbapenem resistance.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by the genetic reconstruction experiments showing that only blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 are required for carbapenem resistance (Table 2). While efflux pump genes are present on pNAR1, the systematic testing of genotypes demonstrates they are not necessary for the resistance phenotype.

results.result: Whole genome sequencing confirmed that pNAR1‾ and pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1 strains had not sustained any other mutations beyond the plasmid changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by whole genome sequencing of the evolved strains, which is essential for confirming that the observed phenotypic changes are due solely to the plasmid modifications and not to additional compensatory mutations.

results.result: Protein analysis of evolved strains A2(o) and A2(t) by SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry showed no consistent changes in both populations to explain the increased imipenem sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by protein analysis (Figure 5F) and mass spectrometry. The negative result is important for ruling out protein-level changes as the primary mechanism and supporting the conclusion that blaDHA-1 loss is the main determinant.

results.result: Only strains with intact pNAR1 (including blaDHA-1) can survive high ceftazidime concentrations. The most logical evolutionary starting point is the genotype without blaDHA-1 or ΔompK36, as it has the highest fitness without antibiotics.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C113 are supported by fitness data across ceftazidime concentrations (Figure 6A) and fitness measurements without antibiotics (Figure 4B). The reasoning about the evolutionary starting point is well-grounded in the fitness data.

results.result: A patient died from septicaemia caused by FK688, which did not respond to carbapenem treatment.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is supported by citation to Bi et al., 2017, which provides the clinical case information. This establishes the clinical significance of the isolate studied.

results.result: Background on antibiotic resistance mechanisms: Antibiotic resistance is driven by selection, carbapenems are reserved for high-risk infections, CRE are widespread globally, and there are two general mechanisms of carbapenem resistance (carbapenemase-mediated and non-carbapenemase). Most K. pneumoniae CRE are caused by carbapenemases, but non-carbapenemase CRE are increasingly recognized, though their mechanisms and evolutionary forces are poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C24 provide established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to surveillance studies, reviews, and primary literature. These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge in the field and provide appropriate context for the study.

results.result: Discussion of the prevalence and clinical context of non-carbapenemase CRE: KPC-2 carbapenemases are widespread in Klebsiella spp., chromosomal β-lactamases are common, plasmids encoding DHA-1 are geographically widespread, ompK35/ompK36 mutations are prevalent, and in some settings up to 55% of CRE may be non-carbapenemase type. Current diagnostic tests target carbapenemases and may miss non-carbapenemase CRE.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C70, C77-C82 are supported by citations to surveillance studies, epidemiological data, and diagnostic test literature. These claims accurately represent the clinical and epidemiological context and are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Treatment implications: Combination therapy with ESBL inhibitors (avibactam or tazobactam) could be effective for non-carbapenemase CRE. Phage therapy for CRE should avoid phages using OmpK35 or OmpK36 as receptors, as this would select for porin defects and inadvertently select for carbapenem resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by citations to clinical studies and are logical inferences from the mechanism of resistance identified in this study. The recommendation about phage therapy is well-reasoned based on the role of porins in both phage entry and carbapenem resistance, supported by citations to phage resistance mechanisms.

results.result: FK688 carries no carbapenemase-encoding genes. The authors used genome sequencing, machine learning (DeepBL), and functional testing in E. coli to identify eight candidate β-lactamases, none of which conferred carbapenem resistance when expressed heterologously.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed the evidence as 'compelling' and noted the study 'offers a set of findings that make a very important contribution.' No concerns were raised about the carbapenemase screening methodology or conclusions.

results.result: Two distinct genetic loci are necessary for carbapenem resistance in FK688: the megaplasmid pNAR1 (carrying blaDHA-1) and an inactivating 48 bp deletion in the chromosomal gene ompK36. Genetic reconstruction experiments confirmed that both loci are required for the resistance phenotype, demonstrating epistasis between blaDHA-1 and ompK36.
results.evaluation: Reviewers described the evidence as 'compelling' and praised the integration of 'experimental and computational approaches.' The genetic reconstruction experiments and structural analysis were not questioned.

results.result: Both resistance loci (blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36) confer significant fitness costs. In experimental evolution without antibiotic selection, FK688 rapidly lost resistance through deletion of blaDHA-1 from pNAR1 or loss of the entire plasmid, restoring carbapenem sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the evidence 'compelling' and noted the study's contribution to understanding 'how antimicrobial resistance evolves.' No concerns were raised about the experimental evolution design or fitness cost measurements.

results.result: Selection in ceftazidime can select for blaDHA-1, potentiating the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single mutation in ompK36. Fitness assays showed that blaDHA-1 is selectively favored even at sub-clinical concentrations of ceftazidime, while the ompK36 mutation is not selected by ceftazidime alone.
results.evaluation: While reviewers praised the data as 'compelling,' they explicitly stated that 'the central claims are not supported' and required authors to 'either provide data on the history of the patient, or substantially reframe the claims made.' The experimental data on sequential selection is strong, but the inference about patient treatment history lacks direct evidence.

results.result: A patient's treatment history might shape the evolution of antibiotic resistance. The evolutionary history of a pathogenic strain can predispose for an AMR phenotype to evolve via specific genetic routes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated 'You must either provide data on the history of the patient, or substantially reframe the claims made' and noted 'the central claims are not supported.' The inference about patient treatment history is not backed by clinical data from the actual patient case.

results.result: The complete genome sequence of K. quasipneumoniae FK688 was generated using short- and long-read sequencing, revealing a circular chromosome (5,211,811 bp) and a novel megaplasmid pNAR1 (1,257,585 bp). This represents the first physical genetic map of a K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae genome.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'combination of experimental and computational approaches' as 'compelling.' No concerns were raised about the genome assembly or phylogenetic classification.

results.result: The fitness defects of blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 are gradually reversed in the presence of increasing imipenem concentrations. Evolved populations lost blaDHA-1 and recovered fitness, with increased carbapenem sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the evidence 'compelling' and did not raise concerns about the fitness assays or evolutionary experiments. The data integration was praised.

results.result: After 200 generations of evolution, samples displayed a mixture of opaque and translucent colony morphotypes. This variation depends on expression of type 1 fimbriae and capsular polysaccharide production.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these observations. The colony morphology data and capsule measurements were part of the 'compelling' evidence package.

results.result: FK688 carries multiple antibiotic resistance determinants on both chromosome and plasmid, including blaOKP-B-21, blaDHA-1, quinolone resistance genes (oqxA, oqxB), fosfomycin resistance (fosA5), and various other resistance genes on pNAR1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the genome analysis as part of the 'compelling' evidence. No concerns were raised about the annotation or identification of resistance genes.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on carbapenemase screening claims (C3, C34-C37, C95-C98). Both evaluations find the evidence compelling and well-supported through comprehensive genome annotation, machine learning predictions, and systematic MIC testing.

Perfect agreement on fitness cost and evolutionary reversibility claims (C5, C28, C44-C47, C49, C67, C75-C76). Both evaluations support the mutation accumulation experiments, competitive fitness assays, and experimental evolution data as compelling evidence.

Strong disagreement on sequential selection and evolutionary pathway claims (C6, C29, C61-C65, C68, C88). OpenEval finds experimental data sufficient to support claims, but peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'central claims are not supported' without patient treatment history data, requiring substantial reframing.

Strong disagreement on patient treatment history inference claims (C7, C87, C89). OpenEval finds experimental demonstration sufficient, but peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly requiring either patient history data or substantial reframing of claims about prior ceftazidime selection.

Perfect agreement on genome annotation and resistance gene identification claims (C31-C33, C71-C72, C91, C103-C104). Both evaluations find the genome analysis compelling with no concerns raised about annotation or resistance gene characterization.

Perfect agreement on colony morphology and capsule-related claims (C55-C58, C108-C110). Both evaluations support the phenotypic observations, genetic data on fimE disruption, and glucuronic acid measurements as part of compelling evidence.

Strong agreement on mechanism of resistance claims involving blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 (C26-C27, C39-C43, C48, C74). Both evaluations find genetic reconstruction, structural analysis, and MIC testing compelling. Peer review includes C4 while OpenEval separates it into R4.

Strong agreement on genome sequencing and phylogenetic classification claims (C25, C30, C66, C90). Both evaluations praise the computational and experimental approaches as compelling. OpenEval additionally includes C2 in this result group.

Strong agreement on fitness recovery and blaDHA-1 loss claims (C52-C54, C59-C60). Both evaluations support the convergent evolution data and genetic reconstruction experiments. Peer review additionally includes C50-C51 in this result group.

Partial overlap on genetic requirement claims (C51). OpenEval groups C4 and C51 together focusing on dual requirement for resistance, while peer review groups C51 with fitness assay claims (C50, C52-C54, C59-C60). Both find evidence compelling.

Partial overlap on concentration-dependent fitness claims (C50). OpenEval groups C50 with C106-C107 focusing on imipenem gradient effects, while peer review groups C50 with broader fitness and evolution claims. Both evaluations support the evidence.
